docs.title: Ella Core
docs.text:
Ella Core is a mobile core designed for private networks. It simplifies the complexity of traditional mobile networks into a single, easy-to-operate solution that is reliable and secure.

Use Ella Core where you need mobile connectivity: in a factory, a warehouse, a farm, a stadium, a ship, a military base, or a remote location.

docs.title: Key features
docs.text:
• 4G and 5G Compliant: Ella Core implements 3GPP-standard interfaces and has been validated with multiple 4G and 5G radios, including integrated and software-defined RANs, commercial phones and devices. It is 5G RedCap compliant for IoT deployments.
  • Performant Data Plane: Achieve high throughput and low latency with an eBPF-based data plane. Ella Core delivers over 10 Gbps of throughput and less than 1 ms of latency.
  • Lightweight: Ella Core is a single binary with an embedded database, making it easy and quick to stand up. It requires as little as 1 CPU core, 1GB of RAM, and 10GB of disk space. Forget specialized hardware; all you need to operate your mobile core network is a Linux system with a network interface.
  • Highly Available: Deploy Ella Core as a high-availability cluster to ensure continuous operation with failover capabilities.
  • Data, Voice, and SMS: Data is built in. Integrate with an IMS for VoLTE and VoNR voice and video calls, and with an SMSC for SMS.
  • Enterprise Network Integration: Plug into your existing network with BGP, VLANs, and VRFs. Define permitted network flows per subscriber, enforce them in the user plane, and track subscriber traffic and usage in real time.
  • AI-Native API: Complete RESTful API and Go client for automation and integration. Manage your network programmatically or let AI agents do it securely using the OpenAPI specification and AI agent skill.
  • Easy to Operate: Manage your private network through a user-friendly embedded web interface. Monitor network health with real-time observability: logs, metrics (Prometheus), traces (OTel), profiles, and dashboards. Keep track of who did what and when with audit logs, and back up and restore your data in 1 click.

docs.title: What is a Mobile Network?
docs.text:
A mobile network connects wireless devices to each other and to the internet.

Mobile Network Overview

docs.title: Components of a Mobile Network
docs.text: A mobile network is broadly divided into two major components: the Core Network and the Radio Access Network (RAN).

docs.title: 1. Core Network
docs.text:
The Core is the heart of a mobile network. It manages all data and signaling flows within the network.

Key Functions of the mobile Core:

  • Authentication and Security: Ensures that devices and users are authenticated and data transmission is secure.
  • Session Management: Establishes and maintains user sessions to provide stable data communication.
  • Policy: Implements quality of service (QoS) rules.
  • Data Network Access: Connects user devices to external data networks like the internet or private networks.

docs.title: 2. Radio Access Network (RAN)
docs.text:
The Radio Access Network (RAN) is the interface between user devices and the core network. It is responsible for transmitting and receiving signals over the air.

Key Components of the RAN

  • Base Station: The base station that connects user equipment (UE) to the core network.
  • Antennas and Spectrum: Handles communication over radio frequencies.

docs.title: The problem with typical Mobile Core Networks
docs.text:
Typical cellular Core networks are designed around a set of specialized components, collectively known as network functions (NFs). Each Network Function serves a specific role. Examples of key 5G network functions include:

  • Access and Mobility Management Function (AMF): Handles registration, connection, and mobility management for user devices.
  • Session Management Function (SMF): Manages session lifecycle and assigns IP addresses to devices.
  • User Plane Function (UPF): Forwards data packets to and from user devices, enabling data transfer between the device and the external network.
  • Authentication Server Function (AUSF): Verifies the identity of users and devices.
  • Network Slice Selection Function (NSSF): Allocates resources for network slicing.

These Network Functions are typically deployed as separate microservices (i.e. separate binaries, configuration files and network connections). However, this approach comes with significant complexity and overhead, including the need for orchestration. This results in high operational costs, that can be prohibitive for private deployments.

A Typical 5G core architecture

docs.title: The Ella Core approach
docs.text:
Ella Core is designed excplicitely and exclusively for private mobile networks. For these users, simplicity, reliability, and security are what counts most. To address these requirements, we made the conscious decision to combine all 4G and 5G network functions into a single application.

Users only interact with Ella Core through a web-based user interface or a REST API, both of which are built into the application.

The Ella Core approach

docs.title: Network Functions are abstracted away
docs.text:
Ella Core still performs the same functions as traditional mobile networks, and towards radios and devices, it implements the same 3GPP standards and protocols. However, HTTP communication between Network Functions is replaced with in-process function calls.

This design greatly simplifies the deployment and operation of the Core network, as there is no need to manage multiple services, databases, or network connections.

docs.title: The database is embedded
docs.text: Persistent data is stored in an embedded database, eliminating the need for managing external databases. This design choice allows for a simple deployment process.

docs.title: Advertising and receiving routes via BGP
Advertising and receiving routes via BGP
What is BGP?
docs.text: BGP is a protocol that allows exchanging routing information between autonomous systems.

docs.title: When is BGP needed?
docs.text: Subscribers receive IPs from the data network pool. When NAT is not used, the external network needs to know how to route packets back to the subscriber through Ella Core. BGP can be needed in enterprise deployments where routable subscriber IPs are required.

docs.title: How does BGP work in Ella Core?
Advertise subscriber routes
docs.text:
Ella Core embeds a BGP speaker that automatically advertises a /32 (IPv4) or /64 (IPv6) route for each active subscriber:

  1. A subscriber establishes a session and receives an IP address (e.g. 10.45.0.3).
  2. Ella Core announces the route 10.45.0.3/32 to all configured BGP peers, with the N6 interface address as the next-hop.
  3. Upstream routers install the route, and return traffic flows through the N6 interface to Ella Core, which delivers it to the subscriber over GTP-U.
  4. When the session is released, Ella Core withdraws the route.

This means routing state always reflects the set of currently connected subscribers with no manual intervention.

Framed routes are advertised the same way, from the node anchoring the session, and withdrawn on release.

The next hop is always the default N6 interface address, so Ella Core advertises only the subscribers whose traffic leaves through that interface: not the IPv4 addresses of subscribers behind NAT, and not the addresses of subscribers on another network instance.

docs.title: Receive routes from BGP peers
docs.text: Ella Core receives routes from BGP peers and installs them into the kernel routing table. This allows operators to manage routes (e.g., a default route via an upstream router) through BGP instead of static routes.

docs.title: In an HA cluster
docs.text: Each node runs its own BGP speaker and advertises /32 (IPv4) or /64 (IPv6) prefixes for the sessions it currently hosts. See High Availability for the broader cluster model.

docs.title: High Availability
docs.text:
High availability (HA) lets you run an Ella Core cluster so that the network keeps working when nodes fail. Each node is active and can accept radios and subscriber traffic.

HA is designed around the Raft Consensus Algorithm: at any time one node is the leader, it is the only node that commits writes, and every write replicates to a majority of voters before it is considered committed. Nodes communicate together via mTLS to share changes.

High Availability in Ella Core

docs.title: Failure tolerance
docs.text:
A cluster keeps accepting writes as long as a majority of its voters are alive. Deploy an odd number of nodes. We recommend 3 or 5, since an even count adds a node without adding tolerance.

Voters Quorum Failures tolerated 3 2 1 5 3 2

Within those bounds, surviving voters keep accepting writes, radio traffic, and operator changes with no manual intervention.

docs.title: What replicates, and what does not
docs.text:
Network-wide resources (subscribers, profiles, policies, slices, data networks, network rules, IP leases, users, API tokens, the operator configuration) replicate across the cluster. If a node dies, the survivors hold the same state, automatically elect a new leader, and keep accepting writes.

Per-node configuration (local data-plane and routing settings) does not replicate. Configure those settings on every node.

Runtime state tied to a specific connection or session also does not replicate: SCTP associations with radios, UE contexts, active sessions and their User Plane state, GTP-U tunnels, and active BGP adjacencies.

Observability is per-node: each instance exposes its own Prometheus endpoint, radio events, flow reports, and audit logs, so operators scrape every node for a cluster-wide view.

docs.title: Failover
docs.text: Each Ella Core node presents as a distinct AMF in the same AMF Set (5G) and a distinct MME in a single MME Pool (4G). A UE's GUTI pins it to the node that handled its registration. When a node dies, radios detect the loss and reselect a surviving AMF/MME. UEs that were attached to the dead node then re-register from scratch, including a fresh authentication and a new session.

docs.title: User plane and routing
docs.text:
A UE's user-plane traffic flows through the node that handled its registration. In an HA cluster, no two UEs receive the same IP address.

When BGP is enabled, each node advertises a /32 (IPv4) or /64 (IPv6) route for every UE session it hosts (see Advertising routes via BGP).

docs.title: Deployment scenarios
docs.text: The HA cluster is the same regardless of how radios connect to it. The radio side determines how much HA reaches individual UEs.

docs.title: Radios connected to every node (AMF Set / MME Pool)
docs.text:
When a node dies, radios reselect within the AMF Set or MME Pool automatically. Affected UEs re-register on a surviving node without operator action.

Radios connected to every node (AMF Set / MME Pool)

docs.title: Radios pinned to specific nodes
docs.text:
Useful for site- or tenant-partitioned deployments. Network-wide state still replicates but if a node dies, its paired radios lose connectivity to the core and must be reconfigured to reach a surviving node.

Radios pinned to specific nodes

docs.title: Roaming
docs.text: Ella Core replicates roaming partner information across the cluster. Each node connects to each roaming partner on its own and serves the roamers it registers, so the partner must accept every node.

docs.title: Draining a node
docs.text:
Draining prepares a node for removal without disrupting traffic on its peers. A draining node signals connected radios so new UEs attach elsewhere, and stops advertising user-plane routes so upstream routing shifts to the survivors.

Drain is triggered by an operator via the cluster API or UI.

docs.title: Scaling the cluster
docs.text:
To scale up, follow the steps in Scale Up a High Availability Cluster.

Shrinking is symmetric. Drain the node, then remove it.

docs.title: Inter-node communication using mTLS
docs.text: Every inter-node connection is mutually authenticated over TLS. Each node owns a long-lived, self-signed cluster certificate. Removing a node immediately revokes its access cluster-wide.

docs.title: Disaster recovery
docs.text: HA clusters recover from total loss through an offline, backup-driven path. An operator stops every node, seeds one node from a backup archive, and starts it. The remaining voters then rejoin with fresh join tokens. The step-by-step procedure lives in Backup and Restore.

docs.title: Rolling upgrades
docs.text:
Upgrades proceed one node at a time: drain the node, refresh its binary, then resume.

Skip-version upgrades (vN → vN+2) and downgrades are not supported.

docs.text:

  • Scale Up a High Availability Cluster — add nodes to an existing cluster.
  • Upgrade — upgrade every node without taking the cluster offline.
  • Cluster API reference — cluster management endpoints.

docs.title: IMS Integration
docs.text: Ella Core lets subscribers make voice and video calls over 4G (VoLTE) and 5G (VoNR). Calls are handled by an external IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS), and Ella Core provides the subscriber data and the Quality of Service (QoS) the IMS needs. The same integration serves other IMS services, such as Mission Critical Push To Talk (MCPTT).

docs.title: What is an IMS?
docs.text:
An IMS is the system that sets up and routes calls in a mobile network. Phones talk to it using SIP, over a regular data session. Its main components are Call Session Control Functions (CSCFs):

  • P-CSCF (Proxy): The phone's first point of contact with the IMS.
  • I-CSCF (Interrogating): Finds the S-CSCF serving a subscriber.
  • S-CSCF (Serving): Registers subscribers and routes their calls.

Ella Core works with any 3GPP-compliant IMS. It has been validated against:

  • Ella IMS
  • Kamailio, which has known deviations from 3GPP and IETF specifications
  • OpenSIPS, which has known deviations from 3GPP and IETF specifications
Ella Core and the IMS

docs.title: The role of Ella Core
docs.text:
Ella Core plays two roles for the IMS, both over Diameter:

Role Interface Used for HSS Cx Subscriber identities, authentication, the S-CSCF assigned to each subscriber, and the application servers that serve them. PCRF / PCF Rx QoS for the media of each call.

Both interfaces are used for 4G and 5G subscribers. The IMS connects to Ella Core's Diameter interface, over SCTP or TCP.

The IMS may address its requests to Ella Core's Diameter realm, epc.mnc<MNC>.mcc<MCC>.3gppnetwork.org, or to its IMS home domain.

docs.title: Allowed IMS peers
docs.text:
A peer matches an allowed IMS peer when it connects from one of its source addresses and, when set, gives its Origin-Host and realm. Matching peers are shown as IMS peers.

Restrict to Allowed Peers, in Integrations › IMS, decides who may connect:

  • Off (the default): any Diameter peer may connect.
  • On: Ella Core rejects the peers that match none, and every peer while no allowed IMS peer is configured. Deleting allowed IMS peers never lets other peers back in.

A peer declares its own Origin-Host and realm, so they identify it but do not prove who it is. Only the source address, and IPsec or TLS between your networks, keep other hosts out. This is why every allowed IMS peer needs at least one source address: an accepted peer can ask Ella Core, as the HSS, for subscribers' IMS authentication data.

docs.title: IMS data networks
docs.text:
An IMS data network carries the phones' SIP signalling and call media. Any data network can be marked as IMS; there can be several, for example ims for phones and a separate one for mission critical devices.

  • P-CSCF discovery: When a phone opens a session on an IMS data network, Ella Core gives it the P-CSCF addresses configured in the IMS settings, of the IP version the phone requested. A changed list applies to new IMS sessions.
  • Signalling QoS: The session's default QoS uses 5QI / QCI 5, the standard class for IMS signalling, or 69 for mission critical signalling.
  • No NAT: Traffic on an IMS data network is never translated, so the IMS can reach phones at their own IP address.
  • UE-to-UE: Traffic between two phones on an IMS data network is always switched locally, so calls between them work without going out N6.

docs.title: IMS identities
docs.text:
Ella Core derives each subscriber's IMS identities from its existing data.

Identity Registration set Format Example Private identity (IMPI) <imsi>@<IMS home domain> 001010100007487@ims.mnc001.mcc001.3gppnetwork.org Public identity (IMPU), default MMTel sip:+<msisdn>@<IMS home domain> sip:+15551230001@ims.mnc001.mcc001.3gppnetwork.org Public identity (IMPU) MMTel tel:+<msisdn> tel:+15551230001 Public identity (IMPU), barred MMTel sip:<imsi>@ims.mnc<MNC>.mcc<MCC>.3gppnetwork.org sip:001010100007487@ims.mnc001.mcc001.3gppnetwork.org Public identity (IMPU) MCPTT sip:mcptt-<msisdn>@<IMS home domain> sip:mcptt-15551230001@ims.mnc001.mcc001.3gppnetwork.org

docs.title: IMS home domain
docs.text:
By default, the IMS home domain is ims.mnc<MNC>.mcc<MCC>.3gppnetwork.org, derived from the operator's PLMN ID. It can be set to another domain, e.g. ims.example.org, which must then match the home domain of the IMS and of the subscribers' ISIMs. Ella Core keeps accepting the derived domain for the private identity and the barred public identity, which phones with a USIM only build from the PLMN ID. The MSISDN and MCPTT identities exist only in the configured home domain.

Changing the home domain moves the application servers' identities to the new domain. It also de-registers subscribers, and the old domain is no longer served.

The phone's IMS client registers the MMTel identities, for voice and SMS. An MCPTT client registers the MCPTT identity, from the same SIM. Both stay registered only if the phone's IMS client registers with a reg-id.

A subscriber without an MSISDN has no usable public identity and cannot make or receive calls.

docs.title: Voice support indication
docs.text:
During registration (5G) or attach and tracking area update (4G), Ella Core tells each phone whether IMS voice is supported. Phones rely on it to decide whether to use VoLTE or VoNR, and some phones refuse to stay on a network that does not indicate it.

Advertise IMS Voice, in Integrations › IMS, controls it:

  • On (the default): Ella Core indicates IMS voice support to every home phone, whatever the IMS configuration.
  • Off: Ella Core never indicates it. Turn it off when no IMS serves voice and your phones fall back to another voice service only when IMS voice is not indicated.

A change reaches each phone at its next registration, attach or tracking area update. Inbound roamers are never told IMS voice is supported, since that requires an IMS voice roaming agreement.

Calls work when:

  • At least one P-CSCF address is configured.
  • The data network named ims, the IMS well-known APN that phones use for voice (GSMA IR.92), exists and is marked as IMS, with an IP pool of the same version as one of the P-CSCF addresses.
  • The subscriber's profile has a policy on the ims data network.
  • The subscriber has an MSISDN.

Integrations › IMS warns when the IMS configuration is not ready for voice. On the Subscriber page, Voice shows the subscriber's voice state and, when voice is off, which condition is missing.

docs.title: Application servers and service profiles
docs.text:
Services such as MCPTT run on application servers: SIP servers that the S-CSCF sends some of a subscriber's requests to. Each application server has:

  • A server name: the SIP URI the S-CSCF sends requests to.
  • Public Service Identities (PSIs): the SIP or tel URIs the server hosts, either distinct or wildcarded to cover a range of identities. Requests addressed to a PSI go straight to its application server.

An IMS service profile is an ordered list of initial filter criteria. A filter criterion sends the requests that match its trigger, such as a SIP method or header, to an application server.

A profile gives its subscribers one service profile for their MMTel identities and one for their MCPTT identity. Without an MCPTT service profile, MCPTT is off.

Changes to service profiles, application servers, or a subscriber's profile reach registered subscribers right away if the S-CSCF supports Cx Push Profile, and at their next re-registration otherwise. Changing or removing a registered subscriber's MSISDN, changing the operator's MCC or MNC or the IMS home domain, or removing the subscriber's access to the IMS de-registers it.

docs.title: MCPTT service profile
docs.text:
The MCPTT service profile has two filter criteria, both to the MCPTT server:

  1. Registration: tells the MCPTT server when a subscriber registers or de-registers. If the MCPTT server can't be reached, the IMS registration still succeeds.
  2. Originating MCPTT sessions: sends the subscriber's MCPTT calls to the MCPTT server. If the MCPTT server can't be reached, the call fails.

Calls from the MCPTT server to subscribers need no filter criteria.

docs.title: Call setup and QoS
docs.text:
1. During call setup, the P-CSCF describes the call's media to Ella Core over Rx: its type, IP addresses, ports, and bandwidth.
  2. Ella Core creates a guaranteed bitrate (GBR) QoS flow (5G) or dedicated bearer (4G) for the media, on the phone's IMS session.
  3. When the call ends, the P-CSCF closes the Rx session and Ella Core releases the QoS flow or bearer.
Media 5QI / QCI ARP priority Voice 1 2 Video 2 4 MCPTT voice and floor control 65 1 to 8, from the call's Resource-Priority

docs.title: MCPTT calls
docs.text:
An MCPTT call's voice and floor control share one GBR QoS flow or bearer with QCI/5QI 65. The session's default QoS flow or bearer on the MC data network uses its policy's QCI/5QI, 5 or 69.

The call's ARP comes from the Resource-Priority the MCPTT server sets.

Resource-Priority ARP priority Pre-emption capability Pre-emption vulnerability mcpttp.<n> 8 − ⌊n / 2⌋, e.g. 1 for mcpttp.15 May pre-empt Not pre-emptable at priority 1 and 2, pre-emptable otherwise mcpttq.<n> 8 − ⌊n / 2⌋ Shall not pre-empt Not pre-emptable at priority 1 and 2, pre-emptable otherwise None 8 Shall not pre-empt Pre-emptable

If a radio pre-empts a session's default QoS flow or bearer, the whole session is released. This is why the MC data network's policy is usually not pre-emptable.

docs.title: EPS fallback
docs.text: Some 5G radios are configured not to carry voice calls. When a voice call starts, such a radio refuses the voice QoS flow and moves the phone to 4G, where Ella Core sets up the call's QoS as a dedicated bearer.

docs.title: In an HA cluster
docs.text:
Each node of a High Availability cluster is a separate Diameter peer of the IMS.

  • Cx: Any node can answer. IMS registrations replicate across the cluster.
  • Rx: Connect the IMS to every node; a call's QoS is set up on the node that holds the phone's session.

docs.title: Managing SIM Cards
docs.text: As a network operator, you will need to provision a SIM card for each subscriber you create in Ella Core. There are two main approaches to managing SIM cards in a private mobile network.

docs.title: Using Physical SIM Cards
docs.text: Physical SIM cards can be used in devices that support them. You will need to obtain blank SIM cards and program them with the subscriber information (IMSI, Key, OPc) corresponding to the subscribers you create in Ella Core.

docs.title: Obtaining SIM Cards
docs.text: You can obtain physical SIM cards from a SIM card vendor (ex. Sysmocom Programmable SIM Cards).

docs.title: Burning SIM Cards
docs.text:
You can burn the SIM card using a card reader/writer (ex. OmniKey 3121) along with software provided by the SIM card vendor. The software will allow you to input the subscriber information (IMSI, Key, OPc) and write it to the SIM card.

For example, using Osmocom's pysim software, you can burn a SIM card with the following command:

export IMSI=001018435063221
export KEY=525c8e65e8449a7067c1ca4367098c60
export OPC=a5db238bfaa2c9f01704332378f10f65
export MCC=001
export MNC=01
export ADMIN_CODE=76543210
./pySim-prog.py -p0 -n Ella -t sysmoISIM-SJA5 -i $IMSI -c $MCC -x $MCC -y $MNC -o $OPC -k $KEY -a $ADMIN_CODE -j 1

SUCI (5G only)

SUCI concealment is a 5G feature. Some devices like iPhones also require the Home Network Public Key to be programmed on the SIM card. When provisioning SUCI support, the SIM must be configured with the protection scheme (Profile A or Profile B), the Key Identifier, and the corresponding public key, matching a home network key configured in Ella Core. You can find the public key on the Operator page in the UI or via the Operator API. If you are using PySim, please refer to the SUCI Concealement documentation.

docs.title: Using eSIM
docs.text: eSIMs (embedded SIMs) allow for remote provisioning of SIM profiles. This can simplify the management of SIM cards, especially in large-scale deployments. You can use an eSIM management platform to create and manage subscriber profiles, which can then be downloaded to eSIM-enabled devices.

docs.title: Obtaining a PLMN ID for a Private Network
Obtaining a PLMN ID for a Private Network
Introduction to PLMN IDs
docs.text:
A Public Land Mobile Network (PLMN) ID is a globally unique identifier that allows mobile devices to recognize and connect to mobile networks. In private mobile networks, having a correct PLMN ID is critical for ensuring proper network identification and operation.

A PLMN ID consists of two parts:

  • Mobile Country Code (MCC): A three-digit code that identifies the country.
  • Mobile Network Code (MNC): A two- or three-digit code that identifies the network operator within that country.

Each subscriber in a mobile network has a unique identifier called the International Mobile Subscriber Identity (IMSI). The IMSI is composed of the PLMN ID and a subscriber-specific identifier.

docs.title: How PLMN IDs Are Assigned
docs.text: PLMN IDs are regulated by the International Telecommunication Union (ITU). Because there is a limited pool of available PLMN IDs, obtaining one through the ITU can be challenging, particularly for private network operators.

docs.title: Options for Private Networks
docs.text:
There are several approaches available for private networks to acquire a PLMN ID:

  1. Using the Reserved PLMN ID: The Mobile Country Code 999 is globally reserved for private networks. Network operators can choose an MNC (e.g., 01, 123) to create a PLMN ID such as 999-01 or 999-123. This method is ideal if your network does not require a globally unique identifier.

  2. National Authority Assignments: In some countries, a designated national regulatory body assigns PLMN IDs to private networks. If your country uses this approach, you must apply for a PLMN ID through the appropriate national channels.

  3. Alliance for Private Networks: The Alliance for Private Networks offers a Network Identifier Program that provides the temporary use of PLMN IDs for private networks. This program allows private network operators to obtain a "slice" of a PLMN ID. They ensure that subscribers from different private networks are uniquely identified and do not overlap.

  4. ITU Assignments: For private networks that require a globally unique identifier, a PLMN ID can be obtained via the ITU process. This typically involves coordination with your local regulatory authority and compliance with international standards.

docs.title: Note on Configuration
docs.text: Once you have obtained a PLMN ID for your private network, you can configure it in Ella Core via the Operator API or the user interface. The PLMN ID can only be updated when no subscribers are created.

docs.title: Platform Security
docs.text:
Info

To report a security vulnerability, please file a Private Security Report.

Security is one of Ella Core's core tenets. From the UI to the database, security is built into every layer of the system.

docs.title: Authentication & Authorization
docs.text:
Ella Core enforces authentication on API requests towards most endpoints. Two authentication methods are supported:

  • Session-based authentication. Users authenticate with email and password. A session cookie and a short-lived access token are issued. The login endpoint enforces per-IP rate limiting.
  • API tokens. Per-user tokens with explicit expiry that can be revoked individually. Recommended for programmatic access.

docs.title: Role-Based Access Control
docs.text:
Every request is authorized against a role-based permission system with three built-in roles:

Role Scope Admin Full access to all resources and operations. Network Manager Manages network resources (subscribers, policies, data networks, routes). Cannot manage users. Read Only Read-only access to network resources.

docs.title: Secret Storage
docs.text:
• User passwords are stored as one-way hashes. Verification uses constant-time comparison.
  • API token secrets are stored as one-way hashes. The raw token is returned only once at creation time and is never retrievable afterward.
  • Session tokens are cryptographically random values. Only a one-way hash is persisted.
  • JWT signing secret is a cryptographically random value generated once and stored in the database. Rotating it invalidates all previously issued tokens and sessions.

docs.title: Transport Security
docs.text:
Ella Core uses TLS to secure its API and web interface.

The TLS configuration is defined in the configuration file. The snap installation generates a self-signed certificate (valid for 365 days) by default. Users can replace the certificate and key files at any time.

For production deployments, replace the self-signed certificate with one issued by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA) and restrict access to the private key.

Ella Core supports TLS 1.2 and 1.3.

In a high-availability cluster, inter-node communication is secured with mutual TLS (TLS 1.3).

docs.title: Minimal Attack Surface
docs.text:
Ella Core minimizes its attack surface through minimal packaging:

  • Container image. Built on a distroless base with no operating system layer, shell, or package manager. Only the strictly necessary runtime dependencies are included. Image size: under 100 MB.
  • Snap. Ships only the application binary and a minimal configuration file. Package size: under 20 MB.

docs.title: Audit Logging
docs.text:
Ella Core logs security-relevant events as audit records that can be accessed via the UI and the API. These logs record who did what and when on your network.

Each audit record contains:

Field Description Timestamp RFC 3339 UTC timestamp. Actor Email of the user who performed the action. Action Machine-readable action identifier (e.g., auth_login). IP Client IP address. Details Human-readable description.

docs.title: Retention
docs.text: Audit logs are retained for 7 days by default. The retention period is configurable through the Audit Logs API.

docs.title: Roaming
docs.text: Ella Core lets subscribers of partner networks attach over 4G and 5G, with Ella Core as the visited network. Their home network authenticates them and holds their subscription. Ella Core carries their traffic to its local data networks (local breakout).

docs.title: Local breakout
docs.text: Ella Core supports local breakout for roaming subscribers, their traffic is routed to the local data networks instead of back to their home network.

docs.title: 5G
docs.text:
In 5G, Ella Core reaches the partner's 5G core through its SEPP, over N32. Each side trusts the other's certificate authority.

5G roaming

docs.title: 4G
docs.text:
In 4G, Ella Core reaches the partner's HSS over S6a, directly or through a Diameter Edge Agent.

4G roaming

docs.title: Roaming partners
docs.text:
A roaming partner is an agreement with another operator. It has:

  • PLMN IDs: the partner's MCC and MNC. Ella Core recognizes the partner's subscribers by their IMSI.
  • A profile: the policy applied to the partner's subscribers, like any profile.
  • A 5G agreement, a 4G agreement, or both: how Ella Core reaches the partner's network.

docs.title: Roamers
docs.text:
A roamer is a subscriber from a partner network who is currently roaming in Ella Core's network.

  • Roamers are listed apart from the subscribers, with their roaming partner.
  • It appears when it registers and disappears when it leaves.
  • Roamers count toward the maximum number of subscribers.
  • Roamers get data service.
  • Deleting a partner deregisters its roamers.

docs.title: In an HA cluster
docs.text: Each node of a High Availability cluster connects to the partner on its own, so the partner must accept every node. See Roaming in an HA cluster.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Configure Roaming — step-by-step guide to add a roaming partner.
  • Integrations API reference — partners, Diameter peers, and SEPP.
  • Roamers API reference — list, inspect, and deregister roamers.
  • 3GPP Compliance — supported roaming procedures.

docs.title: SMS Integration
docs.text:
Ella Core lets subscribers send and receive SMS over 4G and 5G. Messages are stored and forwarded by an external Short Message Service Center (SMSC), such as Ella SMSC. Ella Core works with any 3GPP-compliant SMSC.

A phone exchanges SMS in one of two ways: over NAS, through Ella Core, or over IP, through an IMS.

docs.title: SMS over NAS
docs.text:
SMS over NAS

The message travels inside the signalling between the phone and Ella Core. Ella Core carries it to and from the SMSC, as the MME on 4G or the SMSF on 5G.

As the HSS, Ella Core tells the SMSC where each recipient is served. When a phone that missed messages is reachable again, Ella Core alerts the SMSC.

docs.title: SMS over IP
docs.text:
SMS over IP

The message travels as SIP through the IMS, whose IP-SM-GW carries it to and from the SMSC. Ella Core carries the SIP in the user plane, like any other IMS traffic.

As the HSS, Ella Core sends the SMSC's routing requests to the IP-SM-GW while the phone is registered for SMS over IP. If the IMS cannot deliver a message, the IP-SM-GW sends it through Ella Core over NAS.

docs.title: Who can use SMS
docs.text:
Ella Core allows SMS when:

  • At least one SMSC is configured.
  • Ella Core's serving node number is set. This is the number Ella Core gives the SMSC for itself, as the node serving the phone.
  • The subscriber has an MSISDN.

On 5G, the phone asks for SMS when it registers. On 4G, the phone asks with a combined attach, and Ella Core accepts it for SMS only.

docs.title: SMSCs with several nodes
docs.text: An SMSC can have several Diameter nodes, ex. the members of an Ella SMSC cluster. Ella Core sends each message and alert to one open node, and to the next one if the connection to that node fails. A node that does not answer is avoided for one minute.

docs.title: In an HA cluster
docs.text:
Each node of a High Availability cluster connects to every SMSC node.

  • Receiving: Ella Core answers routing requests with the node that serves the recipient, so the SMSC delivers each message to the right node.
  • Undelivered messages: The record of waiting messages replicates across the cluster, so the node serving the phone when it becomes reachable can alert the SMSC.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Enable SMS — step-by-step guide to enable SMS.
  • Integrations API reference — serving node number and SMSCs.
  • 3GPP Compliance — supported SGd and S6c procedures.
  • Enable SMS over IP — SMS over IP with Ella IMS.

docs.title: Subscriber Security
docs.text:
Info

To report a security vulnerability, please file a Private Security Report.

Ella Core implements 5G-AKA (5G) and EPS-AKA (4G) for secure, mutual authentication between the subscriber's device and the network.

The subscriber's Universal Subscriber Identity Module (USIM) stores the identity and credentials required for authentication:

  • IMSI (International Mobile Subscriber Identity): A globally unique identifier for the subscriber.
  • Key (Subscriber's Secret Key): A 128-bit cryptographic key shared between the USIM and the network.
  • OPc (Operator Code): A value derived from the operator key (OP) and the subscriber's secret key (K) using the Milenage algorithm.
  • SQN (Sequence Number): A counter maintained by both the USIM and the network to prevent replay attacks.

docs.title: Subscriber Privacy (SUCI) - 5G Only
docs.text:
Ella Core supports SUCI (Subscription Concealed Identifier) to protect subscriber identity over the air. The IMSI is encrypted by the subscriber's device before transmission. The network decrypts the SUCI to recover the SUPI. This prevents IMSI-catching attacks.

Two protection profiles are supported:

Profile Curve SUCI Scheme ID Profile A Curve25519 (X25519) 1 Profile B NIST P-256 (secp256r1) 2

Home network keys can be managed through the Operator API or the Operator page in the UI.

docs.title: NAS Security
docs.text:
After authentication, the network and the subscriber's device negotiate ciphering and integrity algorithms. Once established, these algorithms protect all NAS signaling for the lifetime of the connection.

Administrators configure a set of ciphering and integrity algorithms (NULL, SNOW 3G, and AES) and their priority order through the Operator API or the Operator page in the UI.

Warning

Null algorithms (NEA0/NIA0 on 5G, EEA0/EIA0 on 4G) provide no security protection. Only enable them for testing or device compatibility.

docs.title: Managing Subscriber Credentials
docs.text:
Users can update the Operator Key (OP) via the Operator API or the UI.

When creating a new subscriber via the Subscribers API or the UI, Ella Core automatically computes the OPc using the provided Key and the current OP value.

The UI provides a user-friendly interface for automatically generating IMSIs, Keys, and SQNs for new subscribers.

docs.title: User Plane Packet processing with eBPF
Data Plane Packet processing with eBPF
docs.text:
This document explains the key concepts behind Ella Core's subscriber data packet processing.

Ella Core processes subscriber packets between the N3 / S1-U and N6 / SGi interfaces.

docs.title: eBPF, XDP, and TCX
docs.text:
eBPF lets custom programs run in the Linux kernel, and is widely used in networking, security, and performance monitoring.

Ella Core's data plane is an eBPF program, attached at one of two kernel hooks:

  • XDP runs in the network driver, before the kernel builds a socket buffer, and requires driver support.
  • TCX runs later on the socket buffer and is available on every interface.

Attach modes covers the trade-off.

docs.title: Data Plane Packet processing in Ella Core
docs.text:
Ella Core's data plane uses eBPF to achieve high throughput and low latency. Key features include:

  • Policy rules enforcement: Evaluating ordered per-policy uplink and downlink rules to allow or deny traffic based on remote prefix, protocol, and port range.
  • Encapsulation and decapsulation: Managing GTP-U (GPRS Tunneling Protocol-User Plane) headers for data transmission.
  • Rate limiting: Enforcing Quality of Service (QoS) with QER (QoS Enforcement Rules).
  • Flow reporting: Recording per-flow traffic details including source, destination, protocol, port, and whether the flow was allowed or dropped.
  • Usage reporting: Aggregating per-subscriber byte counts for data usage tracking.
  • Statistics collection: Monitoring metrics such as packet counts, drops, and processing times.
Packet processing in Ella Core with eBPF and XDP (Simplified to only show N3->N6).

docs.title: Routing
docs.text: Ella Core relies on the kernel to make routing decisions for incoming network packets. Kernel routes can be configured using the Networking API or the user interface.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Detailed performance results are available here.

docs.title: Attach modes
docs.text:
The data plane can attach at either of two kernel hooks:

  • xdp-native runs in the network driver, before the kernel builds a socket buffer. It is the fastest option, but it needs a driver that supports the hook.

  • tcx runs on the socket buffer, after the kernel's receive path. It is available on every interface, including the veth pairs used in containers and co-hosted deployments. It is the option that always works.

docs.title: Why merged packets must be disabled
docs.text:
tcx runs on the socket buffer, which can hold several packets merged together by the kernel's receive path (GRO, hardware GRO or LRO). Ella Core can't produce valid GTP-U from a merged buffer. On encapsulation, the kernel later splits the buffer back into wire-sized packets and copies the GTP-U header unchanged into each one, so every packet would claim the whole buffer's payload length. On decapsulation, removing the outer headers would remove only the first packet's, and leave the others' GTP-U headers inside the payload. Ella Core drops merged buffers instead, and counts them in app_upf_datapath_drop_total under encap_gso and decap_gso.

To keep those drops from happening, Ella Core turns off packet merging on N3 and N6 before it attaches in tcx mode, so the datapath never sees merged traffic. A feature that the driver or hypervisor fixes on can't be turned off, and Ella Core logs a warning for it.

xdp-native sees each frame before the kernel merges anything. In xdp-generic mode, the kernel itself skips GRO and turns off hardware GRO and LRO on an interface with a generic XDP program, so Ella Core leaves the interface alone.

Two cases remain outside Ella Core's reach:

  • veth: a veth also receives packets merged by its peer when the peer offloads segmentation. That merge happens on the other side of the pair, so it must be turned off on the peer.
  • macvlan and ipvlan: these interfaces receive packets from their lower device, and GRO runs on the lower device before the packets reach them. Changing the macvlan or ipvlan interface has no effect, and the lower device is often in another network namespace or shared with other workloads, so Ella Core logs a warning and leaves it to the operator.

docs.title: XDP redirect on veth pairs
docs.text: When Ella Core's N3 or N6 interface is a veth pair, the data plane redirects packets out of it. In xdp-native mode the veth driver delivers redirected frames only when the receiving peer has an XDP program attached or GRO enabled; otherwise they are dropped. Attaching a minimal XDP_PASS program to the peer is the usual fix. See Use native XDP with veth interfaces for the steps.

docs.title: IPv6 GTP-U transport
docs.text:
GTP-U tunnels on N3 / S1-U run over either IPv4 or IPv6. The inner UE payload family is independent of the outer header family.

Which family is used depends on the interface configuration and on the radio. When N3 is set by name, Ella Core advertises both of the interface's addresses and the radio picks one. When both sides support both families, IPv6 is used. To pin a family, configure N3 with an address of that family.

docs.title: What are VRFs?
docs.text: VRF stands for Virtual Routing and Forwarding. On Linux, they are used to isolate routing and forwarding, using different routing tables. More information can be found in the Linux documentation.

docs.title: How does Ella Core use VRFs?
docs.text:
Ella Core is VRF-aware. It does not itself manage VRFs, but detects their configuration on startup. When they are detected, sockets are bound to the right VRFs, and routes managed by Ella Core through the UI or BGP are set in the right routing tables.

N3 and N6 must always be in the same VRF. Ella Core will refuse to start otherwise. The interface of an additional network instance can be in any VRF.

docs.title: Configuring Ella Core to use VRFs
docs.text: In the configuration file, use the name of the interface that is assigned to the VRF, or use a specific IP address that is assigned to an interface in the VRF.

docs.title: Routing isolation
docs.text:
In Linux by default, if a match is not found when looking up a route in a VRF, the kernel will continue looking up in the main routing table. To prevent this, add a high metric unreachable default route:

ip route add to unreachable 0.0.0.0/0 vrf vrf-name metric 9000

docs.title: Manage Your Network with AI Agents
Manage Your Network with AI Agents
docs.text: Ella Core ships with an Agent Skill that lets AI agents manage your mobile network using natural language. The skill provides the OpenAPI specification so agents can discover and call the REST API on your behalf.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before using the skill, you need:

  1. A running Ella Core instance with its API accessible (e.g. http://192.168.1.10:5000).
  2. A user for your AI agent with an API token. Create a user for your agent in the UI with a role that matches the permissions you want to grant. Then generate an API token for that user and copy it.

docs.title: 1. Install the skill
docs.text:
Claude CodeNPXManual 
/plugin marketplace add ellanetworks/core
/plugin install ella-core@ellanetworks-core

Refresh later with /plugin marketplace update.

Works with any Skills-aware tool that auto-discovers .agents/skills/ (Codex, Cursor, Cline, Goose, Amp, OpenCode, …).

npx skills add ellanetworks/core

Copy the skills/ella-core/ folder into the skills directory your AI tool discovers.

docs.title: 2. Prompt the agent
docs.text:
Once the skill is active, you can ask things like "Which subscribers used the most data over the last 7 days?". The agent will ask you for the Ella Core URL and an API token. Use the token you generated earlier.

Claude Opus responds to "Which subscribers used the most data over the last 7 days?" using its Ella Core skill.

docs.title: Backup and Restore
docs.text: Ella Core stores all persistent data in an embedded database. You can create backups of this database to protect your data and restore it in case of data loss.

docs.title: Backup
docs.text:
1. Open Ella Core in your web browser.
  2. Navigate to the Backup and Restore tab in the left-hand menu.
  3. Click on the Backup button.
  4. The backup file will be downloaded to your computer. It contains sensitive data, store and transfer it encrypted.

Note

This operation can also be done using the API. Please see the backup API documentation for more information.

docs.title: Restore on same instance
docs.text:
Restoring on the same instance will overwrite all existing data in your Ella Core installation. It is only supported on standalone deployments. For High Availability deployment, see the disaster recovery procedure.

  1. Open Ella Core in your web browser.
  2. Navigate to the Backup and Restore tab in the left-hand menu.
  3. Click on the Upload File button.
  4. Select the backup file you want to restore.

Note

This operation can also be done using the API. Please see the restore API documentation for more information.

docs.title: Offline Restore (Disaster Recovery)
docs.text:
This procedure can be used on new instances.

Paths below assume the default data directory /var/snap/ella-core/common/data (the directory holding db.path).

  1. Stop the daemon on every node in the cluster, or the single standalone node:

    sudo snap stop ella-core.cored

  2. On the node you seed from the backup, delete the old cluster state:

    sudo rm -rf /var/snap/ella-core/common/data/ella.db \
            /var/snap/ella-core/common/data/ella.db-wal \
            /var/snap/ella-core/common/data/ella.db-shm \
            /var/snap/ella-core/common/data/raft \
            /var/snap/ella-core/common/data/cluster-tls

  3. Drop the backup archive into the data directory as restore.bundle:

    sudo cp backup.tar.gz /var/snap/ella-core/common/data/restore.bundle
sudo chmod 600 /var/snap/ella-core/common/data/restore.bundle

  4. Start the daemon on that node:

    sudo snap start --enable ella-core.cored

  5. For a Standalone deployment, stop here.

  6. On each remaining node, repeat step 2, then add it via the join-token flow.

docs.title: Advertise subscriber routes with BGP
docs.text:
Ella Core includes an embedded BGP speaker that advertises /32 (IPv4) or /64 (IPv6) routes for each active subscriber. This guide walks through enabling BGP, adding a peer, and verifying the configuration.

NAT must be disabled

Ella Core does not advertise the IPv4 addresses of subscribers on a data network with NAT, nor the addresses of subscribers on a network instance other than default. Disable NAT on the data networks to advertise, in the Slices section of each data network's page, before proceeding.

docs.title: Enable BGP
docs.text:
1. Open the Ella Core UI and navigate to Networking > BGP.
  2. Edit the BGP settings:
    • Local AS: Your autonomous system number (e.g. 64512).
    • Router ID: A unique IPv4 address identifying this BGP speaker. Leave it empty to use the N6 interface current IPv4 address (e.g. 192.168.5.10).
    • Listen Address: The address and port to listen on (default :179). Leave the address empty to accept sessions on every interface, or set one to restrict the speaker to it. Change the port only if you need BGP on a non-standard one. When VRFs are in use, this address also scopes peer connections: set it to an address on a VRF-enslaved interface and both the listener and all peers are bound to that VRF; leave it empty and both follow the N6 interface's VRF.
  3. Click Save.
  4. Toggle BGP to ON.

docs.title: Add a BGP peer
docs.text:
1. In the Networking > BGP tab, scroll to the Peers section.
  2. Click Create.
  3. Fill in the peer details:
    • Address: The IP address of the upstream router (e.g. 192.168.5.1 or 2001:db8::1).
    • Remote AS: The AS number of the peer (e.g. 64513).
    • Hold Time: BGP hold timer in seconds (default 90). The keepalive interval is derived as hold time / 3 per RFC 4271.
    • Password (optional): MD5 authentication password. Must match the peer's configuration.
    • Description (optional): A label for the peer.
  4. Click Create.

docs.title: Verify advertised routes
docs.text: View the advertised subscriber routes in the Advertised Routes table. The next-hop is always the N6 interface address.

docs.title: Configure the upstream router
docs.text:
Ella Core advertises routes, and can receive them from peers via each peer's import prefixes. You still need to configure the upstream router to:

  1. Peer with Ella Core (matching the AS number and address configured above).
  2. Accept all routes for subscriber data networks (e.g. 192.168.0.0/24 or 2001:db8::/32)
  3. Accept framed-route prefixes, if any are configured (e.g. 192.168.60.0/24).

Consult your router's documentation for BGP peering configuration.

Note

All steps in this guide can also be performed via the REST API. See the BGP API reference for details.

docs.title: Co-host with Ella IMS and Ella SMSC
Co-host with Ella IMS and Ella SMSC
docs.text: This guide runs Ella IMS and Ella SMSC on the same host as Ella Core. Ella IMS runs in its own network namespace, which Ella Core reaches through an N6 network instance.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
To follow this guide, you will need:

  • A host with Ella Core installed with the snap, as in Install, and an eth0 interface towards the radio and the internet.
  • A free address on the LAN for Ella IMS's UI.

The examples use these values:

Value Role eth0 Host interface: N2, N3, N6, and the Ella Core and Ella SMSC UIs 10.3.0.2 Ella Core's Diameter address 10.3.0.7 Ella SMSC's Diameter address 10.6.0.2 Ella Core's address on the ims network instance 10.6.0.5 Ella IMS's SIP and Diameter address 192.168.1.50/24 Ella IMS's UI address on the LAN 192.168.1.1 LAN gateway 10.46.0.0/16 IP pool of the ims data network 001 / 01 Ella Core's MCC and MNC epc.mnc001.mcc001.3gppnetwork.org Ella Core's Diameter realm +15550000000 Ella SMSC's service centre address 15550000100 Ella IMS's IP-SM-GW number

docs.title: 1. Create the Ella IMS network namespace
docs.text:
Create /etc/systemd/system/ims-netns.service:

[Unit]
Description=Ella IMS network namespace
Wants=network-online.target
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=oneshot
RemainAfterExit=true

ExecStartPre=-ip netns delete ims
ExecStartPre=-ip link delete diameter0
ExecStart=ip link add diameter0 type dummy
ExecStart=ip addr add 10.3.0.2/32 dev diameter0
ExecStart=ip addr add 10.3.0.7/32 dev diameter0
ExecStart=ip link set diameter0 up
ExecStart=ip netns add ims
ExecStart=ip link add n6-ims type veth peer name ims0
ExecStart=ip link set ims0 netns ims
ExecStart=ip addr add 10.6.0.2/24 dev n6-ims
ExecStart=ip link set n6-ims up
ExecStart=ip link add lan0 link eth0 type macvlan mode bridge
ExecStart=ip link set lan0 netns ims
ExecStart=ip -n ims link set lo up
ExecStart=ip -n ims addr add 10.6.0.5/24 dev ims0
ExecStart=ip -n ims link set ims0 up
ExecStart=ip -n ims addr add 192.168.1.50/24 dev lan0
ExecStart=ip -n ims link set lan0 up
ExecStart=ip -n ims route add default via 192.168.1.1 dev lan0
ExecStart=ip -n ims route add 10.3.0.0/24 via 10.6.0.2 dev ims0
ExecStart=ip -n ims route add 10.46.0.0/16 via 10.6.0.2 dev ims0 mtu lock 1400
ExecStart=ip netns exec ims ethtool -K ims0 tso off gso off tx off
ExecStop=-ip netns delete ims
ExecStop=-ip link delete diameter0

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Enable and start the service:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now ims-netns.service

docs.title: 2. Configure Ella Core
docs.text:
Edit /var/snap/ella-core/common/core.yaml:

logging:
  system:
    level: "info"
    output: "stdout"
  audit:
    output: "stdout"
db:
  path: "/var/snap/ella-core/common/data/ella.db"
interfaces:
  n2:
    name: "eth0"
  n3:
    name: "eth0"
  n6:
    name: "eth0"
  network-instances:
    - name: "ims"
      n6:
        name: "n6-ims"
  api:
    address: "0.0.0.0"
    port: 5002
  diameter:
    address: "10.3.0.2"
datapath:
  attach-mode: "tcx"
telemetry:
  enabled: false

Create /etc/systemd/system/snap.ella-core.cored.service.d/override.conf:

[Unit]
Requires=ims-netns.service
After=ims-netns.service

Restart Ella Core:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo snap restart ella-core.cored

docs.title: 3. Install Ella IMS in the namespace
docs.text:
Install Ella IMS:

sudo snap install ella-ims
sudo snap connect ella-ims:network-control

Edit /var/snap/ella-ims/common/ims.yaml and set its addresses:

api:
  address: 0.0.0.0
  port: 5020
sip:
  addresses: [10.6.0.5]
diameter:
  address: 10.6.0.5

Create /etc/systemd/system/snap.ella-ims.imsd.service.d/override.conf:

[Unit]
Requires=ims-netns.service
After=ims-netns.service

[Service]
NetworkNamespacePath=/var/run/netns/ims

Start Ella IMS:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo snap start --enable ella-ims.imsd

Ella IMS's UI is at http://192.168.1.50:5020.

docs.title: 4. Install Ella SMSC
docs.text:
Install Ella SMSC:

sudo snap install ella-smsc

Edit /var/snap/ella-smsc/common/smsc.yaml and set its Diameter address:

diameter:
  address: 10.3.0.7

Create /etc/systemd/system/snap.ella-smsc.smscd.service.d/override.conf:

[Unit]
Requires=ims-netns.service
After=ims-netns.service

Start Ella SMSC:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo snap start --enable ella-smsc.smscd

Ella SMSC's UI is at http://<eth0 address>:5010.

docs.title: 5. Connect Ella IMS to Ella Core
docs.text:
In the Ella IMS UI, go to the Operator page:

  • Click the edit icon next to Operator ID (MCC/MNC), enter 001 / 01, and click Update.
  • Click the edit icon next to Numbering Plan, enter your country code and prefixes, and click Update.

Go to the Cores page:

  • Under Peers, click Add Peer, enter 10.3.0.2, check HSS and PCRF, and click Add.
  • Under HSS, click the edit icon next to HSS Realm, enter epc.mnc001.mcc001.3gppnetwork.org, and click Update.
  • Under Voice QoS, click the edit icon next to Policy Function, select PCRF, and click Update.
  • Click the edit icon next to PCRF Realm, enter epc.mnc001.mcc001.3gppnetwork.org, and click Update.

docs.title: 6. Connect Ella SMSC to Ella Core
docs.text:
In the Ella SMSC UI, go to the Operator page:

  • Click the edit icon next to Operator ID (MCC/MNC), enter 001 / 01, and click Update.
  • Click the edit icon next to Service Centre Address, enter +15550000000, and click Update.
  • Click the edit icon next to Numbering, enter your country code and prefixes, and click Update.

Go to the Diameter page and note the Host, e.g. smsc.node.epc.mnc001.mcc001.3gppnetwork.org.

In the Ella Core UI, go to Integrations › SMS. Click the edit icon next to Serving Node Number, enter Ella Core's E.164 number for SMS, e.g. +15550001111, and click Update. Then click Add SMSC and enter:

  • Name: smsc
  • Service Centre Addresses: +15550000000
  • Address: 10.3.0.7
  • Origin-Host: Ella SMSC's Host.

Click Add.

docs.title: 7. Enable SMS over IP
docs.text:
In the Ella IMS UI, go to the Cores page:

  • Under SMS over IP, click the edit icon next to IP-SM-GW Number, enter 15550000100, and click Update. Note the IP-SM-GW Name.
  • Under Peers, click Add Peer, and enter:
    • Address: 10.3.0.7
    • Roles: SGd only
    • Service Centres: 15550000000
    • Transport: SCTP
    • Host: Ella SMSC's Host.
  • Click Add.
  • Click the edit icon of the 10.3.0.2 peer, check Sh, S6c and SGd, and click Update.

In the Ella Core UI, go to Integrations › IMS:

  • Click Add Application Server, enter ip-sm-gw as the Name and Ella IMS's IP-SM-GW Name as the Server Name, and click Add.
  • Click Add Service Profile, enter sms-over-ip as the Name. Under Add from preset, select the SMS over IP preset and the ip-sm-gw Application Server, click Add Criteria, and click Add.

docs.title: 8. Route the ims data network to Ella IMS
docs.text:
In the Ella Core UI:

  1. Go to Networking > Data Networks, click Create, enter ims as the Name and 10.46.0.0/16 as the IPv4 Pool, turn on IMS (voice and mission critical services), and click Create.
  2. Open the ims data network. In Slices, select the slice of your subscribers and click Serve on slice, then set its Network instance to ims.
  3. Go to Integrations › IMS, click the edit icon next to P-CSCF Addresses, enter 10.6.0.5, and click Update.

docs.title: 9. Set up the subscribers
docs.text:
In the Ella Core UI, for each profile whose subscribers make calls and send SMS:

  • Go to the Profiles page and open the profile.
  • Click Add Policy, enter a Name, set the Data Network to ims, and click Create.
  • Click the edit icon next to IMS Service Profiles, set MMTel (voice, SMS) to sms-over-ip, and click Save.

For each subscriber, go to the Subscribers page, open the subscriber, click the edit icon next to MSISDN, enter its E.164 number, e.g. +15551230001, and click Update.

On each SIM card, set the SMSC number to +15550000000. On each phone, turn on VoLTE (4G) or VoNR (5G).

docs.title: 10. Verify
docs.text:
• In the Ella Core UI, go to Networking > Interfaces: the N6 (External) · ims card shows n6-ims, used by ims.
  • In the Ella IMS UI, go to Cores: under Peers, 10.3.0.2 and 10.3.0.7 show open.
  • In the Ella SMSC UI, go to Diameter: under Connected Peers, Ella Core and Ella IMS show open.
  • In the Ella Core UI, go to Subscribers and open a subscriber with an MSISDN: Voice shows Registered.
  • Call a phone from another. The call connects with audio in both directions.
  • Send an SMS between two phones. In the Ella SMSC UI, on the Messages page, it shows delivered.

docs.title: Co-host with OCUDU
docs.text:
Ella Core can be hosted with radio software like OCUDU (previously known as srsRAN) to operate an all-in-one private mobile network. This guide provides step-by-step instructions to deploy Ella Core alongside OCUDU using a Linux network namespace.

Co-host Ella Core with OCUDU

Note

The same instructions can be used to co-host Ella Core with srsRAN 4G.

docs.title: Pre-requisites
docs.text:
To follow this guide, you will need:

  • Ubuntu Server 26.04
  • A host with a wired network interface
  • A USB, UHD-compatible SDR

The instructions below were written for a Raspberry Pi 5 running Ubuntu 26.04 and the Ettus Research B205-mini SDR. Please adapt the interface names and SDR configuration as needed for your setup.

Tip

OCUDU requires some performance tuning for stable operation, especially on resource-constrained hosts like a Raspberry Pi. We recommend the following optimizations for OCUDU performance:

  • Use Ubuntu Real-Time (following documentation)
  • Use a high real-time scheduling priority (with chrt)

docs.title: 1. Install Ella Core and OCUDU
docs.text:
Install Ella Core using the How-to Install guide and install OCUDU using the snap:

sudo snap install ocudu
sudo snap connect ocudu:kernel-module-observe
sudo snap connect ocudu:process-control
sudo snap connect ocudu:network-control
sudo snap connect ocudu:system-observe
sudo snap connect ocudu:raw-usb

docs.title: 2. Create a network namespace for N3
docs.text:
Create a linux network namespace n3ns for the N3 interface between OCUDU and Ella Core.

Install the OCUDU performance script:

sudo curl -o /usr/local/bin/ocudu_performance https://gitlab.com/ocudu/ocudu/-/raw/dev/scripts/ocudu_performance
sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/ocudu_performance

Create /etc/systemd/system/n3ns.service:

[Unit]
Description=N3 Network Setup
Wants=network-online.target
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=oneshot
RemainAfterExit=true

ExecStartPre=-ip netns delete n3ns
ExecStart=ip netns add n3ns
ExecStart=ip link add n3-upf-veth type veth peer name n3-ran-veth
ExecStart=ip link set n3-ran-veth netns n3ns
ExecStart=ip addr add 10.202.0.3/24 dev n3-upf-veth
ExecStart=ip -n n3ns addr add 10.202.0.5/24 dev n3-ran-veth
ExecStart=ip -n n3ns link set lo up
ExecStart=ip -n n3ns link set dev n3-ran-veth up
ExecStart=ip link set dev n3-upf-veth up
ExecStart=ip netns exec n3ns ethtool -K n3-ran-veth tso off gso off
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/ocudu_performance -y
ExecStop=-ip netns delete n3ns

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Enable and start the service:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now n3ns.service

Make sure eth0 is not optional in /etc/netplan/50-cloud-init.yaml:

network:
  version: 2
  ethernets:
    eth0:
      dhcp4: true
      optional: false

Apply the Netplan configuration:

sudo netplan apply

docs.title: 3. Configure Ella Core
docs.text:
Configure Ella Core's N3 and N3 interfaces to use the n3ns namespace and set N6 to the physical interface eth0:

logging:
  system:
    level: "debug"
    output: "stdout"
  audit:
    output: "stdout"
db:
  path: "/var/snap/ella-core/common/data/ella.db"
interfaces:
  n2:
    name: "n3-upf-veth"
    ngap-port: 38412
  n3:
    name: "n3-upf-veth"
  n6:
    name: "eth0"
  api:
    address: "0.0.0.0"
    port: 5002
datapath:
  attach-mode: "tcx"
telemetry:
  enabled: false

Note

We use tcx mode here because the Raspberry Pi 5 does not support native XDP. Use xdp-native if you can and follow the Use native XDP with veth interfaces guide to attach an XDP program to the peer veth.

Create the override file /etc/systemd/system/snap.ella-core.cored.service.d/override.conf:

[Unit]
Requires=n3ns.service
Wants=network-online.target
After=n3ns.service network-online.target

Reload systemd and start Ella Core:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo snap start --enable ella-core.cored

docs.title: 4. Configure OCUDU
docs.text:
Configure OCUDU's CU to use the n3ns namespace:

cu_cp:
  amf:
    addr: 10.202.0.3
    port: 38412
    bind_addr: 10.202.0.5
    supported_tracking_areas:
      - tac: 1
        plmn_list:
          - plmn: "99901"
            tai_slice_support_list:
              - sst: 1
  inactivity_timer: 300
  security:
    nea_pref_list: nea2,nea1
    nia_pref_list: nia2,nia1
cu_up:
  ngu:
    socket:
      - bind_addr: 10.202.0.5
ru_sdr:
  device_driver: uhd
  device_args: type=b200
  clock: internal
  srate: 23.04
  tx_gain: 80
  rx_gain: 40

cell_cfg:
  dl_arfcn: 665000
  band: 77
  channel_bandwidth_MHz: 20
  common_scs: 30
  plmn: "99901"
  tac: 1
  pdcch:
    dedicated:
      ss2_type: common
      dci_format_0_1_and_1_1: false
  prach:
    prach_config_index: 160
  pdsch:
    mcs_table: qam64
  pusch:
    mcs_table: qam64

log:
  filename: stdout
  all_level: warning

pcap:
  mac_enable: disable
  ngap_enable: disable

Save this configuration to /var/snap/ocudu/common/gnb.yml.

Override the ocudu gnb service by writing /etc/systemd/system/snap.ocudu.gnb.service.d/override.conf:

[Service]
NetworkNamespacePath=/var/run/netns/n3ns

Enable and start OCUDU:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo snap start --enable ocudu.gnb

You should see the LEDs light up on your USRP, and see the radio appear in Ella Core's UI.

You can validate OCUDU is running properly by looking at the logs:

sudo snap logs ocudu -n 1000 -f

docs.title: Configure Roaming
docs.text: This page has two guides: 5G roaming and 4G roaming. Each adds a roaming partner, so the partner's subscribers can attach to Ella Core. To learn how roaming works, see Roaming.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Data networks and slices: a data network named after each DNN that the partner's subscribers use, e.g. internet (names match regardless of letter case), and slices with the S-NSSAI values of their subscriptions, each serving these data networks.
  • Partner subscriptions: the partner allows local breakout for these data networks in its subscriptions.

docs.title: 1. Enable the N32 interface
docs.text:
On each node, set interfaces.n32 in the configuration file to the interface that reaches the partner's SEPP:

interfaces:
  n32:
    address: "192.0.2.11"
    port: 443

Restart Ella Core.

docs.title: 2. Exchange information with the partner
docs.text:
On each node, go to Integrations › Roaming. Under This Core, note the SEPP FQDN from the Certificate row, and the N32 Address.

Give the partner:

Item Example Your PLMN ID 001/01 Each node's SEPP FQDN and N32 address sepp1.5gc.mnc001.mcc001.3gppnetwork.org, 192.0.2.11:443 The trust anchors, downloaded from the Trust anchor row sepp-ca.pem

Get from the partner:

Item Example Its PLMN IDs 999/70 Its SEPP FQDN sepp1.5gc.mnc070.mcc999.3gppnetwork.org Its N32-c URI https://sepp1.5gc.mnc070.mcc999.3gppnetwork.org:443 Its trust anchor partner-ca.pem The NRF API root of each of its PLMN IDs https://nrf.5gc.mnc070.mcc999.3gppnetwork.org

Configure DNS so that Ella Core resolves the partner's SEPP FQDN, and the partner resolves each node's SEPP FQDN.

docs.title: 3. Create a profile for roamers
docs.text:
Go to the Profiles page and create a profile named roamers, with 5G access.

Add a policy on each data network that roamers may use, e.g. internet.

docs.title: 4. Add the partner
docs.text:
In Integrations › Roaming, open Partners and click Add Partner:

  • Name: e.g. Partner Telecom.
  • MCC and MNC: the partner's PLMN ID, e.g. 999 and 70. Click Add PLMN for each other PLMN ID of the partner.
  • Profile: roamers.
  • 5G Roaming: turn on, and enter the partner's SEPP FQDN, N32-c URI, Trust Anchor, and the NRF API Root of each PLMN ID.

Click Create.

docs.title: 5. Verify
docs.text:
On each node, in Integrations › Roaming, the partner shows Established in the N32 Status column of Partners.

Register a 5G UE with a SIM of the partner's network, with data roaming on. Open the Roamers tab of the Subscribers page of the node that serves it: the roamer appears, with its roaming partner.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Data networks: a data network named after each APN that the partner's subscribers use, e.g. internet (names match regardless of letter case), served on a slice.
  • Partner subscriptions: the partner allows local breakout for these APNs in its subscriptions.

docs.title: 1. Exchange information with the partner
docs.text:
Give the partner:

Item Example Your PLMN ID 001/01 The Diameter Realm, from Integrations › Roaming, under This Core epc.mnc001.mcc001.3gppnetwork.org Each node's Origin-Host, from the same place mmec01.mmegi0001.mme.epc.mnc001.mcc001.3gppnetwork.org Each node's Diameter address and port (interfaces.diameter) 192.0.2.11, 3868

Get from the partner:

Item Example Its PLMN IDs 999/70 The address and SCTP port of its HSS or Diameter Edge Agent 198.51.100.5, 3868

docs.title: 2. Create a profile for roamers
docs.text:
Go to the Profiles page and create a profile named roamers, with 4G access.

Add a policy on each data network that roamers may use, e.g. internet.

docs.title: 3. Add the Diameter peer
docs.text:
In Integrations › Roaming, open Diameter Peers and click Add Diameter Peer:

  • Address: the partner's HSS or Diameter Edge Agent, e.g. 198.51.100.5.
  • Port: e.g. 3868.

Click Create.

docs.title: 4. Add the partner
docs.text:
Open Partners and click Add Partner:

  • Name: e.g. Partner Telecom.
  • MCC and MNC: the partner's PLMN ID, e.g. 999 and 70. Click Add PLMN for each other PLMN ID of the partner.
  • Profile: roamers.
  • 4G Roaming: turn on, and select the Diameter peer from step 3.

Click Create.

docs.title: 5. Verify
docs.text:
On each node, in Integrations › Roaming, the partner's Diameter peer shows Connected under Diameter Peers.

Attach a 4G UE with a SIM of the partner's network, with data roaming on. Open the Roamers tab of the Subscribers page of the node that serves it: the roamer appears, with its roaming partner.

Note

All steps in this guide can also be performed via the REST API. See the Integrations API reference for details.

docs.title: Deploy a High Availability Cluster
docs.text: Ella Core can be deployed as a high-availability cluster to provide redundancy and failover capabilities. See High Availability for more information.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Three hosts meeting the standard system requirements.
  • Ella Core installed on each host via the Install guide with cluster.bind-address set in the configuration file.

docs.title: 1. Start node 1
docs.text: Start node 1, open a browser at the API address and initialize it normally.

docs.title: 2. Create a join token for node 2
docs.text: Still in node 1, open the Cluster page and click Add Node, click Mint Token, then copy the token.

docs.title: 3. Start node 2
docs.text: Start node 2, open a browser at the API address and click Join an existing cluster instead. Paste the token, enter node 1's cluster address, and click Join.

docs.title: 4. Add node 3
docs.text: Repeat steps 2 and 3 for node 3.

docs.title: 5. Verify
docs.text: On the Cluster page, all three nodes appear as Healthy.

docs.title: Deploy in the Cloud
docs.text:
Run Ella Core in the cloud while your radios stay on site. Deploy a three-node cluster across three zones and connect a radio to it over IPsec.

Note

This guide uses cloud instances. Ella Core can also run on managed Kubernetes, such as GKE or EKS.

Google CloudAWSAzure

Ella Core running in Google Cloud

Ella Core running in AWS

Ella Core running in Azure

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A radio that supports IPsec and several MME or AMF addresses. Without IPsec on the radio, use an IPsec router at the site.
Google CloudAWSAzure
  • A Google Cloud project and the gcloud CLI.

The examples use 203.0.113.10 for the site's public address, 192.168.1.50 for the radio, and 10.128.0.0/20 for the default subnet in us-central1.

  • An AWS account and the aws CLI.

The examples use 203.0.113.10 for the site's public address, 192.168.1.50 for the radio, and the default VPC (172.31.0.0/16) in us-east-1.

  • An Azure subscription and the az CLI, with the bastion and ssh extensions.
  • An SSH key at ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.

The examples use 203.0.113.10 for the site's public address, 192.168.1.50 for the radio, and 10.10.0.0/16 for the virtual network in eastus.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the project
docs.text:
Google CloudAWSAzure

Set the project and region:

gcloud config set project <project>
R="--region us-central1"

Allow the radio to reach Ella Core:

gcloud compute firewall-rules create ella-core-allow-radio --network default \
  --allow sctp:36412,sctp:38412,udp:2152,icmp \
  --source-ranges 192.168.1.50/32 --target-tags ella-core

Allow the nodes to reach each other:

gcloud compute firewall-rules create ella-core-allow-cluster --network default \
  --allow tcp:7000 --source-tags ella-core --target-tags ella-core

Allow Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) to reach SSH and the UI:

gcloud compute firewall-rules create ella-core-allow-iap --network default \
  --allow tcp:22,tcp:5002 --source-ranges 35.235.240.0/20 --target-tags ella-core

Give the instances internet access:

gcloud compute routers create ella-nat-router --network default $R
gcloud compute routers nats create ella-nat --router ella-nat-router $R \
  --auto-allocate-nat-external-ips --nat-all-subnet-ip-ranges

Set the region and find the default VPC:

export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
VPC=$(aws ec2 describe-vpcs --filters Name=isDefault,Values=true --query 'Vpcs[0].VpcId' --output text)

Allow the radio to reach Ella Core, and the nodes to reach each other:

SG=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name ella-core --description "Ella Core" --vpc-id $VPC --query GroupId --output text)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id $SG --ip-permissions \
  'IpProtocol=132,IpRanges=[{CidrIp=192.168.1.50/32}]' \
  'IpProtocol=udp,FromPort=2152,ToPort=2152,IpRanges=[{CidrIp=192.168.1.50/32}]' \
  'IpProtocol=icmp,FromPort=-1,ToPort=-1,IpRanges=[{CidrIp=192.168.1.50/32}]' \
  "IpProtocol=tcp,FromPort=7000,ToPort=7000,UserIdGroupPairs=[{GroupId=$SG}]"

Allow Session Manager to reach the instances:

aws iam create-role --role-name ella-core-ssm --assume-role-policy-document \
  '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"ec2.amazonaws.com"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole"}]}'
aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name ella-core-ssm --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore
aws iam create-instance-profile --instance-profile-name ella-core-ssm
aws iam add-role-to-instance-profile --instance-profile-name ella-core-ssm --role-name ella-core-ssm

Create the resource group:

az group create -n ella-core -l eastus
G="-g ella-core"

Create the virtual network, with subnets for the instances, the VPN gateway and Bastion:

az network vnet create $G -n ella-vnet --address-prefixes 10.10.0.0/16 --subnet-name ella --subnet-prefixes 10.10.1.0/24
az network vnet subnet create $G --vnet-name ella-vnet -n GatewaySubnet --address-prefixes 10.10.255.0/27
az network vnet subnet create $G --vnet-name ella-vnet -n AzureBastionSubnet --address-prefixes 10.10.254.0/26

Give the instances internet access:

az network public-ip create $G -n ella-nat-ip --sku StandardV2 --allocation-method Static
az network nat gateway create $G -n ella-nat --sku StandardV2 --public-ip-addresses ella-nat-ip
az network vnet subnet update $G --vnet-name ella-vnet -n ella --nat-gateway ella-nat

Create a Bastion host to reach SSH and the UI:

az network public-ip create $G -n ella-bastion-ip --sku Standard
az network bastion create $G -n ella-bastion --vnet-name ella-vnet --public-ip-address ella-bastion-ip \
  --sku Standard --enable-tunneling

docs.title: 2. Create the VPN gateway
docs.text:
Google CloudAWSAzure

Create a Classic VPN gateway:

gcloud compute addresses create radio-vpn-ip $R
GW=$(gcloud compute addresses describe radio-vpn-ip $R --format='value(address)')
echo $GW
gcloud compute target-vpn-gateways create radio-vpn --network default $R
gcloud compute forwarding-rules create radio-vpn-esp $R --address $GW --target-vpn-gateway radio-vpn --ip-protocol ESP
gcloud compute forwarding-rules create radio-vpn-udp500 $R --address $GW --target-vpn-gateway radio-vpn --ip-protocol UDP --ports 500
gcloud compute forwarding-rules create radio-vpn-udp4500 $R --address $GW --target-vpn-gateway radio-vpn --ip-protocol UDP --ports 4500

Create a pre-shared key, the tunnel, and a route to the radio:

head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64 | tr -d '/+=' | head -c 32 > radio-vpn.psk
gcloud compute vpn-tunnels create radio-tunnel $R --target-vpn-gateway radio-vpn \
  --peer-address 203.0.113.10 --ike-version 2 --shared-secret "$(cat radio-vpn.psk)" \
  --local-traffic-selector 10.128.0.0/20 --remote-traffic-selector 192.168.1.50/32
gcloud compute routes create radio-route --network default --destination-range 192.168.1.50/32 \
  --next-hop-vpn-tunnel radio-tunnel --next-hop-vpn-tunnel-region us-central1

Create a virtual private gateway and attach it to the VPC:

VGW=$(aws ec2 create-vpn-gateway --type ipsec.1 --query VpnGateway.VpnGatewayId --output text)
aws ec2 attach-vpn-gateway --vpn-gateway-id $VGW --vpc-id $VPC
until [ "$(aws ec2 describe-vpn-gateways --vpn-gateway-ids $VGW --query 'VpnGateways[0].VpcAttachments[0].State' --output text)" = attached ]; do sleep 5; done
RT=$(aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC Name=association.main,Values=true --query 'RouteTables[0].RouteTableId' --output text)
aws ec2 enable-vgw-route-propagation --route-table-id $RT --gateway-id $VGW

Create a customer gateway for the site, a pre-shared key, the VPN connection, and a route to the radio:

CGW=$(aws ec2 create-customer-gateway --type ipsec.1 --ip-address 203.0.113.10 --bgp-asn 65000 --query CustomerGateway.CustomerGatewayId --output text)
head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64 | tr -d '/+=' | head -c 31 | sed 's/^/k/' > radio-vpn.psk
T='{"IKEVersions":[{"Value":"ikev2"}],"PreSharedKey":"'$(cat radio-vpn.psk)'","Phase1EncryptionAlgorithms":[{"Value":"AES256"}],"Phase2EncryptionAlgorithms":[{"Value":"AES256"}],"Phase1IntegrityAlgorithms":[{"Value":"SHA2-256"}],"Phase2IntegrityAlgorithms":[{"Value":"SHA2-256"}],"Phase1DHGroupNumbers":[{"Value":14}],"Phase2DHGroupNumbers":[{"Value":14}]}'
VPN=$(aws ec2 create-vpn-connection --type ipsec.1 --customer-gateway-id $CGW --vpn-gateway-id $VGW \
  --options '{"StaticRoutesOnly":true,"LocalIpv4NetworkCidr":"192.168.1.50/32","RemoteIpv4NetworkCidr":"172.31.0.0/16","TunnelOptions":['"$T,$T"']}' \
  --query VpnConnection.VpnConnectionId --output text)
aws ec2 create-vpn-connection-route --vpn-connection-id $VPN --destination-cidr-block 192.168.1.50/32
GW=$(aws ec2 describe-vpn-connections --vpn-connection-ids $VPN --query 'VpnConnections[0].VgwTelemetry[0].OutsideIpAddress' --output text)
echo $GW

Create the VPN gateway. This can take 45 minutes:

az network public-ip create $G -n radio-vpn-ip --sku Standard --zone 1 2 3
az network vnet-gateway create $G -n radio-vpn --vnet ella-vnet --public-ip-addresses radio-vpn-ip \
  --gateway-type Vpn --vpn-type RouteBased --sku VpnGw1AZ
GW=$(az network public-ip show $G -n radio-vpn-ip --query ipAddress -o tsv)
echo $GW

Create a local network gateway for the site, a pre-shared key, and the connection:

az network local-gateway create $G -n radio-site --gateway-ip-address 203.0.113.10 --local-address-prefixes 192.168.1.50/32
head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64 | tr -d '/+=' | head -c 32 > radio-vpn.psk
az network vpn-connection create $G -n radio-tunnel --vnet-gateway1 radio-vpn --local-gateway2 radio-site \
  --shared-key "$(cat radio-vpn.psk)"
az network vpn-connection ipsec-policy add $G --connection-name radio-tunnel \
  --ike-encryption AES256 --ike-integrity SHA256 --dh-group DHGroup14 \
  --ipsec-encryption AES256 --ipsec-integrity SHA256 --pfs-group PFS2048 \
  --sa-lifetime 27000 --sa-max-size 102400000

docs.title: 3. Create the instances
docs.text:
Google CloudAWSAzure

Create one instance per zone, at 10.128.0.10, 10.128.0.11 and 10.128.0.12:

i=10
for z in a b c; do
  gcloud compute instances create ella-core-$z --zone us-central1-$z \
    --machine-type e2-standard-2 --subnet default --private-network-ip 10.128.0.$i \
    --no-address --tags ella-core \
    --image-family ubuntu-2404-lts-amd64 --image-project ubuntu-os-cloud \
    --boot-disk-size 20GB
  i=$((i+1))
done
